abstract: Cerebellar transcranial alternating current stimulation (ctACS) can improve motor learning and may speed rehabilitation. The mechanisms by which ctACS induces long-term changes in brain function that underlie these effects are not known, and knowledge of them could greatly improve the application of ctACS. One potential mechanism is alteration of Purkinje cell (PC) complex spike (CS) activity, as CS activity is a key regulator of cerebellar synaptic plasticity. Thus, we investigated how ctACS modifies CS firing rates and waveform. Extracellular recordings were obtained from cerebellar PCs in anesthetized adult rats while ctACS (250 A) was applied across a range of frequencies (0.5 - 50 Hz). The effect of ctACS on CS waveform was quantified via measuring changes in the overall size of the CS and in the number and amplitude of the spikelets that comprise a CS. ctACS produced phase-dependent modulation of the CS waveform in a majority of PCs at most tested frequencies, with 1 Hz stimulation causing modulation in all PCs tested at the frequency. The modulation reflected changes within the normal range of CS waveforms rather than an expansion of that range. Analysis of individual spikelet periods (windows) revealed that ctACS modified discrete portions of the CS, with 93.8% of PCs showing significant modulation in at least one window. Notably, the strength of phase-dependent CS waveform modulation was relatively consistent across frequencies, in contrast to the frequency dependence of simple spike (SS) entrainment. Significant modulation of spikelet amplitude was found more often than that of spikelet number; however, the relative strength of the modulation when present was similar for the two parameters. CS waveform modulation was correlated with SS entrainment strength and was strongest in PCs located near the cerebellar surface (i.e., near the apices of the folia). Together, these findings demonstrate that ctACS exerts phase-dependent control over CS waveform. Moreover, the differing frequency dependence of the waveform effects and SS firing modulation suggests that it may be possible to target CS-related plasticity selectively, providing a potential strategy for selectively modulating cerebellar learning with ctACS.
